question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer, CIO of Aravalli Long-Short Fund (a Cat III open-ended AIF), is explaining onboarding material to a prospective HNI family office. The family currently parks INR 40 crore in 91-day T-bills 'as savings' and another INR 60 crore in the fund unit class. Which statement BEST captures the saving-versus-investment distinction as articulated in the NISM chapter?

answer.text: Savings and investment are interchangeable because both involve setting aside money earned over money spent.

Saving is simply income minus expenditure typically parked in highly-liquid short-term instruments, while investment is a current commitment of that saving to specific asset classes with a longer horizon expecting a higher return.
Every saver is automatically an investor the moment the money enters a bank deposit, irrespective of time horizon.
Investment is defined as any capital allocation to equity instruments only, while saving covers debt instruments only.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 1 Section 1.1.1 separates the two: saving is the residual (earnings minus spending) typically held in short-term liquid instruments, while investment is the commitment of those savings for a specific time period with an expectation of a higher return. The chapter states 'every investor is a saver but not vice versa.' Parking in T-bills is saving-mode; the Cat III long-short unit class is investment-mode. The Trap: Option A reflects the loose usage the chapter explicitly rejects. Option C reverses the 'every investor is a saver, not vice versa' logic. Option D fabricates an asset-class boundary that the chapter does not draw — both equity and debt can sit on either side depending on horizon and intent. Note: The saving-versus-investment distinction is defined in Chapter 1 by horizon and intent, not by the instrument used.
